analysis.one_liner: Bans the manufacture and sale of handguns deemed unsuitable for sporting purposes, such as cheap concealed-style pistols.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote in the House Judiciary Committee and died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it a federal crime to manufacture, assemble, transfer, or possess any handgun that the Treasury Secretary determines is unsuitable for lawful sporting purposes, using standards already in federal law. Handguns people legally owned before the law passed would have been exempt. The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its crime subcommittee, which never acted on it before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Communities affected by handgun violence, especially areas where inexpensive, easily concealable handguns are common; the bill aimed to shrink the supply of such guns going forward.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People in communities affected by gun violence

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful for any person to manufacture, assemble, transfer, or possess any handgun the Treasury Secretary determines unsuitable for lawful sporting purposes, applying existing federal sporting-purposes standards to cheap, concealable handguns.
Grandfathers possession of any handgun lawfully owned before enactment, so current owners would not have to surrender their guns.

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers and sellers of inexpensive, easily concealable handguns, who would lose the civilian market for those products; buyers of those guns in the future.

drawbacks.text: The bill gives the Treasury Secretary broad discretion to decide which handguns are 'unsuitable for sporting purposes,' which gun-rights supporters saw as a way to ban whole categories of handguns by executive determination rather than by explicit legislation.

The ban applies only to future manufacture and transfers and exempts guns already owned, so it would leave millions of prohibited handguns in circulation for years and would not by itself remove guns already on the street.
Critics argued the sporting-purposes standard targets inexpensive handguns most used for self-defense by lower-income people, who would face fewer affordable options.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was a modest, targeted measure: it would have cut off the future supply of cheap concealable handguns without touching guns people already owned. The cost falls on a small segment of the gun industry and on future buyers of those specific guns, while the public-safety benefit depends on how aggressively the Treasury Secretary used the designation power. Its main design weakness is that it relies heavily on executive discretion and grandfathers existing weapons.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Judiciary Committee and its crime subcommittee for the rest of the Congress and was never scheduled for a vote, dying when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Rep. Lawrence Smith of Florida introduced the Handgun Violence Prevention Act of 1989 on April 15, 1991, with 16 original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Judiciary the same day it was introduced.
On June 7, 1991, it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime and Criminal Justice, where it remained without further action.
The bill gathered 31 cosponsors, 28 Democrats and 3 Republicans, but never reached the House floor before the Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers and sellers of inexpensive handguns kept their market, and no restriction was placed on any handgun during the Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Cheap handgun makers kept their market

for.name: Rep. Lawrence Smith
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban handguns unsuitable for lawful sporting purposes and pressed for cosponsors.

for.name: 31 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, 28 Democrats and 3 Republicans.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee and Subcommittee on Crime and Criminal Justice
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral in April 1991, never holding a markup or sending it to the floor.

against.name: National Rifle Association
against.what_they_did: Opposed legislation restricting handgun availability during this era and lobbied against gun-control measures in Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan but lopsided: 28 Democrats and 3 Republicans cosponsored, and the record does not show floor votes, so the partisan shape of opposition cannot be measured.

industries.note: The bill would make it illegal to manufacture or transfer any handgun the Treasury deems unsuitable for sporting purposes, which historically covers cheap, easily concealable pistols. These manufacturers would lose the civilian market for those products.

Dealers would be barred from transferring newly banned handguns, shrinking their sellable inventory of low-cost handguns going forward. Existing lawfully owned guns remain transferable under the grandfather clause.
The bill would expand federal discretion to restrict handgun ownership, which gun-rights groups opposed as a precedent for broader bans.
